tweets.text:
you are making video games all wrong

for decades almost all game art time went into reverse-engineering the end result

you start with concept art of what you WANT it to look like. then for YEARS you walk the computer backwards into something it can process: a rendering engine, 3d assets that fit that engine, and a gamer’s local hardware that has to turn all of that back into a high fidelity image

incredibly slow. incredibly expensive. but it was the best we had

ai makes that pipeline faster as everyone is figuring out today. but they’re missing the real unlock:

YOU DON’T NEED THAT PIPELINE AT ALL

if you have a reference for the end look, you don’t model it in 3d. you don’t reverse-engineer into an engine

you keep a very basic greybox model of the world as the source of truth, and track every entity in real time. it doesn’t need to look good at all… the player never sees it!

a fast video model turns that into the “game” in real time. it doesn’t have to look like a game. it can look like a 2d cartoon or cinematic live action

@fal’s h3 max is very fast. astra 6 low-effort too. neither is fully realtime yet but together they can generate continuous, coherent, player-controlled scenes, faster than playback

early demo:

yeah, so, let’s say early 2d street fighter games, the entire gameplay loop of button mashing was influenced by the tech: you had to have 2d sprites with animated fight moves because that’s the only thing the engines could do. then hopefully if you’re a reasonable player you control your character correctly such that it looks and plays like an actual fight and not like 2 guys standing meters apart from each other punching air

then modern adaptations recreated the same game loop in more procedural and semantic 3d worlds. but it’s still the same game loop based on technical constraints of the 90s

the thing is, a modern video model doesn’t have any of these problems at all. it’s never gonna have a guy punching air in the corner, because it understands the world and the action and generates something that makes sense

but you won’t control it by button mashing anymore. the control scheme will be different and most importantly the core loop will be very different because it is no longer designed backwards from the limitations of 90s game engines

$PONS is now up 375x from its lows just 1.5 months ago.

it ran from a 250k mcap to nearly hitting unicorn status today.

it was fairly distributed and available onchain from the start. everyone had the exact same chance, and more than enough time to add it to their portfolios.

thanks to bear market ptsd, most people stayed completely sidelined (myself included). and even most of those who caught it early sold way too soon, locking in solid profit but still missing a generational run.

it took a runner like this for people to wake up and start believing in something again. the bear market is over, and there are still plenty of once in a lifetime opportunities sitting completely overlooked, just waiting to get picked up.

make the most of the next few months. these windows are rare.

#Uranium #Silver #Copper #Gold

DAILY METALS PULSE | SEPTEMBER 6, 2026

The weekend just reset the risk picture.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships. Iran says it also targeted three tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent had already closed Friday at $96.28, its highest since July 24.

🥇 GOLD

Gold was hit Friday after 162,000 new US jobs pushed the implied probability of a September Fed hike to roughly 65%. Spot gold fell to around $4,419.

Now a fresh safe-haven catalyst has arrived. The tension is clear: geopolitical risk supports gold, while higher oil can fuel inflation, yields and the dollar.

🥈 SILVER

Silver fell to around $65.83 alongside gold. It should share any renewed safe-haven demand, but its higher beta means volatility could be considerably greater. The structural shortage story remains intact.

🟠 COPPER

Copper held near $14,400/t and was heading for a tenth consecutive weekly gain. Shanghai inventories fell 13% to 63,000 tonnes, the lowest since January 2024.

War escalation may pressure growth-sensitive copper initially, but tight physical availability outside the US remains the dominant structural signal.

☢️ URANIUM

Uranium remained quiet at approximately $89.50/lb.

There was no fresh weekend supply-and-demand bombshell, but renewed danger around Hormuz keeps sulphur and sulphuric-acid logistics risk alive for acid-intensive uranium production. No new disruption has been confirmed.

The temporary ceasefire enabling repairs at Zaporizhzhia is welcome nuclear-safety news, but neutral for uranium fundamentals.

BOTTOM LINE:

Gold and silver enter the week with a fresh safe-haven catalyst. Copper faces a serious risk-off test while inventories remain tight. Uranium remains the calmest, and perhaps cleanest, structural story of the four.

With US cash markets closed Monday for Labor Day, early price action may be noisy. Next week’s inflation data will determine whether the Fed or geopolitics takes control.

One optimistic and still very-non-consensus belief I have about the far future of cryptography:

I think that there is a 33% chance that, for average real-world computation, there exist ways to implement all three of what I call the Egyptian God Protocols (SNARK, FHE, iO) with 1+ε factor overhead (meaning, for large enough instances, the added overhead of cryptographizing a computation becomes arbitrarily small compared to the base cost of doing the computation itself)

And a 60% chance that all three can be done with single-digit overhead (ie. <10x, measured in total cost of energy plus amortized compute)

I think there's a good chance we'll get one of these (probably SNARKs with single-digit overhead) by the end of this decade. After all, we're already there for specialized hash functions and for some LLM inference.

Many years of hard work went into the Poseidon family of hashes, and they have provided great real-world value on Ethereum and elsewhere and will continue to do so for several years. They are the reason why it's fast to generate a client-side SNARK for a modern privacy-protocol.

The fact that we have ultra-fast general-purpose STARKs (mid-three-digit overhead for basically any batched computation) and may well soon drop to double-digit or even lower is more amazing than anything that we had been hoping for in the early 2020s.

Big congratulations to all involved in Poseidon, and all involved in STARKs.
 https://t.co/cdERDYkj6n

𝐀𝐌𝐄𝐑𝐈𝐂𝐀 𝐌𝐔𝐒𝐓 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐓𝐑𝐎𝐋 𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐎𝐖𝐍 𝐀𝐈 𝐅𝐔𝐓𝐔𝐑𝐄

America must be very careful.

There is a growing debate about whether building data centers is worth the pressure they place on electricity grids, water supplies, and local communities.

These concerns are legitimate. Every major industrial expansion has costs, and data-center developers should be required to address them honestly. But America must not confuse refusing to build infrastructure with eliminating the demand for it.

If the United States blocks data centers at home, the need for computing power will not disappear. The data centers will simply be built somewhere else. Along with them will go the investment, jobs, technological capacity, and, most importantly, control.

That is not environmental leadership. It is the outsourcing of strategic dependence.

Europe has already shown us the danger of this approach.

For years, much of Europe reduced its domestic energy production while becoming increasingly dependent on imported Russian gas. In 2021, Russia supplied approximately 45% of the European Union’s gas imports.

The arrangement appeared economically rational. Europe received relatively cheap energy while keeping much of the environmental and geopolitical cost conveniently outside its borders.

Then Russia invaded Ukraine.

Europe’s dependence on Russian energy did not, by itself, cause the war. But it gave Russia enormous leverage, restricted Europe’s choices, and may have influenced Putin’s calculation that Europe would hesitate to impose serious consequences.

Energy that Europe had treated as an ordinary commodity suddenly revealed itself as a strategic weapon.

Europe eventually responded. It imposed sanctions, found alternative suppliers, and dramatically reduced its dependence on Russian fuel.

But the adjustment came at an enormous economic cost, after the vulnerability had already been exposed.

The lesson is not that international trade is bad.

The lesson is that a country should think very carefully before placing infrastructure essential to its security in the hands of others.

Artificial intelligence now presents America with a similar strategic choice.

Data centers are not merely large buildings filled with servers. They are becoming the factories of intelligence.

They will power scientific research, military systems, financial markets, medicine, communications, and almost every important industry.

A country that controls computing capacity, reliable energy, and the physical infrastructure connecting them controls an essential part of its future.

This does not mean America should approve every proposed facility or allow companies to ignore local communities.

Data centers should pay appropriately for the power and infrastructure they consume. Developers should invest in additional power generation, transmission, storage, and water-efficient cooling. Local communities should share in the economic benefits rather than simply absorb the costs.

But there is a profound difference between regulating construction responsibly and making construction impossible.

If America chooses the second path merely to make its domestic emissions look lower, it will not make the world cleaner.

It will simply move the emissions and infrastructure elsewhere, potentially to countries with weaker environmental standards, while surrendering the jobs and strategic advantage as well.

A clean national balance sheet can be an accounting illusion when the dirty work has merely been moved abroad.

The atmosphere does not care on which side of a border the electricity was generated.

National security, however, cares deeply about who controls the power, the chips, the networks, and the computing capacity.

The world is not perfect. Every serious decision involves trade-offs.

1/2

Europe’s dependence on Russian energy did not, by itself, cause the war. But it gave Russia enormous leverage, restricted Europe’s choices, and may have influenced Putin’s calculation that Europe would hesitate to impose serious consequences.

Energy that Europe had treated as an ordinary commodity suddenly revealed itself as a strategic weapon.

Europe eventually responded. It imposed sanctions, found alternative suppliers, and dramatically reduced its dependence on Russian fuel.

But the adjustment came at an enormous economic cost, after the vulnerability had already been exposed.

The lesson is not that international trade is bad.

The lesson is that a country should think very carefully before placing infrastructure essential to its security in the hands of others.

Artificial intelligence now presents America with a similar strategic choice.

Data centers are not merely large buildings filled with servers. They are becoming the factories of intelligence.

They will power scientific research, military systems, financial markets, medicine, communications, and almost every important industry.

A country that controls computing capacity, reliable energy, and the physical infrastructure connecting them controls an essential part of its future.

This does not mean America should approve every proposed facility or allow companies to ignore local communities.

Data centers should pay appropriately for the power and infrastructure they consume. Developers should invest in additional power generation, transmission, storage, and water-efficient cooling. Local communities should share in the economic benefits rather than simply absorb the costs.

But there is a profound difference between regulating construction responsibly and making construction impossible.

If America chooses the second path merely to make its domestic emissions look lower, it will not make the world cleaner.

It will simply move the emissions and infrastructure elsewhere, potentially to countries with weaker environmental standards, while surrendering the jobs and strategic advantage as well.

A clean national balance sheet can be an accounting illusion when the dirty work has merely been moved abroad.

The atmosphere does not care on which side of a border the electricity was generated.

National security, however, cares deeply about who controls the power, the chips, the networks, and the computing capacity.

The world is not perfect. Every serious decision involves trade-offs.

1/2

2/2

Countries that refuse to acknowledge this often congratulate themselves for appearing virtuous while becoming dependent on countries that are less constrained and far less friendly.

Europe learned that energy independence cannot be replaced by good intentions. America should not learn the same lesson about artificial intelligence after it is too late.

Build the power.
Build the data centers.
Address the environmental costs honestly.

And maintain control over the infrastructure that will define the next economic and geopolitical era.

America must control its own destiny.
